column2: The first step in determining if evidence for a claim is convincing is to:
column3: Show that the observed results are consistent with the claim being investigated
column4: Prove that the population parameter exactly equals the value of the sample statistic
column5: Calculate the population proportion directly from the raw data that were collected
column6: Demonstrate that the sample was collected using a stratified random sampling method

column2: In significance testing, the two possible explanations for an observed result are:
column3: The result occurred by random chance alone, or there is a real underlying effect
column4: The sample was too small for the study, or the sample was too large for the test
column5: The population is normally distributed, or the population is not normally distributed
column6: The parameter is equal to the statistic, or the parameter differs from the statistic

column2: A simulation in significance testing helps us determine:
column3: How likely the observed result is to occur by chance if there were no real effect
column4: The exact numerical value of the population parameter we are trying to estimate
column5: Whether the data were collected using an appropriately randomized sampling method
column6: How many additional observations are needed to reach a definitive final conclusion

column2: If a simulation shows that the observed result happens frequently by chance alone, we conclude:
column3: The evidence is not convincing because random chance is a plausible explanation
column4: The evidence is convincing because many simulated trials confirmed the observed result
column5: The experiment was poorly designed and needs to be repeated with many more subjects
column6: The treatment definitely has no real effect on the outcome that is being measured

column2: Evidence for a claim is considered 'convincing' when:
column3: Random chance can be eliminated as a plausible explanation for the observed result
column4: The sample proportion is at least somewhat larger than the hypothesized proportion
column5: At least half of all simulated results closely match the observed result obtained
column6: The sample size exceeds 30 and the collected data appear normally distributed

column2: A simulation shows that only 2 out of 1000 trials produced a result as extreme as what was observed. This suggests:
column3: The observed result is very unlikely by chance alone, providing convincing evidence
column4: The simulation was most likely done incorrectly and should be carefully repeated
column5: The researcher needs a much larger sample before drawing any meaningful conclusions
column6: The observed result is consistent with what we would expect if there were no effect

column2: A simulation shows that 320 out of 1000 trials produced a result as extreme as what was observed. This suggests:
column3: The observed result could easily have occurred by chance, so evidence is not convincing
column4: The evidence is moderately convincing since fewer than half of all trials matched it
column5: The treatment has a 32% probability of working on members of the general population
column6: The sample size was approximately the correct amount needed for this particular study

column2: In significance testing, we compare our observed result to what would happen:
column3: If there were no real effect and any observed differences were due to chance alone
column4: If the treatment worked on every single subject in exactly the same measurable way
column5: If we used a much larger sample that was selected from a different target population
column6: If we repeated the identical experiment under perfectly controlled laboratory conditions

column2: 'By chance alone' in significance testing means the result that would occur if:
column3: The claim were false and the observed differences are due only to random variation
column4: We made a computational error when calculating the sample statistic from raw data
column5: The population parameter shifted in value between the time of sampling and analysis
column6: Our sample happened to be biased due to an unintentional flaw in the study design

column2: The logic of significance testing is used throughout Units 6 through 9 to:
column3: Evaluate whether collected data provide convincing evidence for a statistical claim
column4: Calculate exact population parameters from sample statistics with no remaining error
column5: Determine the minimum sample size needed for any statistical procedure to be valid
column6: Identify whether a variable being studied is categorical or quantitative in nature

column2: The two major types of statistical inference are:
column3: Confidence intervals to estimate parameters and significance tests to evaluate claims
column4: Point estimates to find exact values and interval estimates to find plausible ranges
column5: Descriptive statistics to summarize data and inferential statistics to make predictions
column6: Sampling distributions to model variation and probability distributions to assign likelihood

column2: When the goal is to estimate a single population proportion, the appropriate procedure is:
column3: A one-sample z-interval for a population proportion
column4: A two-sample z-interval for a difference in proportions
column5: A one-sample t-interval for a population mean
column6: A chi-square test for goodness of fit

column2: The 'Random' condition for constructing a confidence interval ensures that:
column3: The sample is representative so that results can be generalized to the population
column4: The sample proportion will always be very close to the true population proportion
column5: The sampling distribution will have a standard deviation that is less than one
column6: The margin of error will be smaller than the confidence level that was chosen

column2: The 10% condition (n ≤ 10% of N) is checked when sampling without replacement because:
column3: Sampling a large fraction of a population without replacement affects independence
column4: The sample must contain at least 10% of the population to produce useful results
column5: The margin of error formula is only mathematically valid when n is at most 10% of N
column6: The confidence level must always be adjusted when samples exceed 10% of the population

column2: The Large Counts condition requires np̂ ≥ 10 and n(1 − p̂) ≥ 10 because this:
column3: Ensures the sampling distribution of the sample proportion is approximately normal
column4: Guarantees that the sample was selected randomly from the population of interest
column5: Confirms that the true population proportion falls between 0.10 and 0.90 inclusive
column6: Verifies that the sample size is large enough relative to the total population size

column2: If a study uses a convenience sample rather than a random sample, the confidence interval:
column3: May not be valid because the sample might not be representative of the population
column4: Will still be valid but will always produce a wider margin of error than expected
column5: Will work correctly provided that the other two required conditions are fully met
column6: Should be calculated using a t-distribution instead of the standard z-distribution

column2: A sample has 45 successes and only 5 failures out of 50 observations. Which condition is NOT met?
column3: The Large Counts condition, because the number of failures is less than 10
column4: The Random condition, because convenience sampling was used to collect data
column5: The 10% condition, because the sample is too large relative to the population
column6: All three conditions are satisfied since the total sample size is at least 30

column2: Conditions for inference must be verified BEFORE performing any calculations because:
column3: The formulas and conclusions are valid only when the underlying assumptions are met
column4: Checking conditions is faster than completing the full confidence interval calculation
column5: The conditions determine which specific calculator function should be used for it
column6: The AP exam gives extra credit for showing condition verification before any work

column2: A confidence interval has the general form:
column3: Point estimate plus or minus the margin of error for the given confidence level
column4: Population parameter plus or minus the standard deviation of the original data
column5: Sample size multiplied by the estimated probability of success in the population
column6: Critical value divided by the square root of the estimated sample proportion

column2: The margin of error in a confidence interval is calculated as:
column3: The critical value multiplied by the standard error of the sample statistic
column4: The sample proportion divided by the total number of observations in the sample
column5: The population proportion minus the sample proportion, then squared and summed
column6: The confidence level expressed as a decimal multiplied by the total sample size

column2: The standard error of p̂ estimates:
column3: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion
column4: The average distance between the sample proportion and the value of zero
column5: The probability that the confidence interval will fail to capture the parameter
column6: The total range of all possible sample proportions from the same population

column2: We use p̂ instead of p in the standard error formula for a confidence interval because:
column3: We don't know the true population proportion — that is what we're trying to estimate
column4: The sample proportion is always a more accurate value than the population proportion
column5: Using p would give a standard error that is larger than what p̂ would produce
column6: Statistical convention requires that sample statistics be used in all inference work

column2: A critical value (z*) determines:
column3: How many standard errors wide the interval must be for the desired confidence level
column4: The probability that the sample proportion equals the true population proportion
column5: Whether the sampling distribution is approximately normal or noticeably skewed
column6: The minimum number of observations required to construct a valid confidence interval

column2: Increasing the confidence level from 90% to 99% while keeping sample size the same will:
column3: Increase the critical value and produce a wider confidence interval overall
column4: Decrease the critical value and produce a narrower confidence interval overall
column5: Not change the width of the interval but will change the interpretation given
column6: Increase the standard error of the statistic but decrease the margin of error

column2: A confidence interval of (0.45, 0.63) for a population proportion means:
column3: We are confident the true population proportion is captured between 0.45 and 0.63
column4: Exactly 45% to 63% of individuals in the population have the characteristic studied
column5: The sample proportion was 0.45 and the calculated margin of error was 0.63
column6: There is a 45% to 63% probability that this particular interval is correct

column2: The margin of error in a confidence interval tells us:
column3: How much the sample statistic is likely to vary from the true population parameter
column4: The probability that the confidence interval successfully contains the true parameter
column5: The difference between the largest and smallest observed values in the sample
column6: The number of standard deviations between the sample mean and the interval boundary

column2: 'We are 95% confident' in the context of confidence intervals means:
column3: About 95% of intervals made this way from repeated samples would capture the parameter
column4: There is a 95% probability that the true parameter is inside this specific interval
column5: Exactly 95% of the individuals in the sample fall within the interval boundaries
column6: The sample proportion is within 95% of the exact value of the population proportion

column2: A confidence interval for a proportion can be used to evaluate a claim by checking:
column3: Whether the claimed value falls inside or outside the calculated confidence interval
column4: Whether the sample proportion is larger or smaller than the value being claimed
column5: Whether the margin of error is greater or less than the specific claimed value
column6: Whether the confidence level is higher or lower than the stated significance level

column2: When all other factors remain the same, increasing the sample size will:
column3: Decrease the margin of error and produce a narrower confidence interval
column4: Increase the margin of error and produce a wider confidence interval
column5: Change the confidence level but will not affect the interval width
column6: Have no predictable effect on the resulting width of the confidence interval

column2: The width of a confidence interval for a proportion is exactly equal to:
column3: Twice the margin of error
column4: The standard error of the sample proportion
column5: The critical value squared
column6: Half the total sample size

column2: When planning a study and determining sample size before data collection, we may use p̂ = 0.5 because:
column3: It produces the largest possible margin of error, providing a safe upper bound for n
column4: It is the most common value of population proportions found in real-world studies
column5: The sample size formula only works correctly when p̂ is set to exactly 0.5
column6: It makes the standard error equal to zero, which simplifies the calculation

column2: When solving for minimum sample size and the result is n ≥ 246.3, you should use:
column3: n = 247, rounding up to guarantee the margin of error stays within the requirement
column4: n = 246, rounding down to the nearest whole number as is standard practice
column5: n = 246.3 exactly, since sample size does not need to be a whole number value
column6: n = 2463, multiplying by 10 because of the 10% condition for independence

column2: A researcher wants a narrower confidence interval without changing the confidence level. She should:
column3: Increase the sample size, which will reduce the standard error of the statistic
column4: Decrease the sample size, which will reduce the overall margin of error
column5: Switch to a completely different population that has less natural variability
column6: Replace the confidence interval procedure with a significance test instead

column2: The confidence interval formula for a proportion does not need to be memorized because:
column3: It can be built from the general CI form and standard error formula on the formula sheet
column4: The AP exam always provides the fully worked-out formula for each specific problem
column5: Statistical calculators automatically determine the correct formula from the data
column6: Only the final numerical answer matters on the exam, not the formula that was used

column2: A 95% confidence interval for a population proportion is (0.52, 0.68). Which conclusion is best supported?
column3: There is convincing evidence that the population proportion is greater than 0.50
column4: There is convincing evidence that the population proportion is exactly 0.60
column5: There is no evidence about the population proportion since this is just an estimate
column6: The population proportion is definitely between 0.52 and 0.68 with no uncertainty
